question:
A junior risk analyst at an Australian fund of funds (AUD 850 million) monitors a USD share class of a US equity fund using the style benchmark with shorting,

$\text{r}_{\text{t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f ,t}+1} = \alpha_{\text{t}} + \beta_{\text{SPY,t}} \left(\text{SPY}_{\text{t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f ,t}+1}\right) + \text{h}_{\text{t}} (\text{SPYV}_{\text{t}}+_{1} - \text{SPYG}_{\text{t}}+_{1}) + \epsilon_{\text{t}}+_{1}$.

The loadings estimated at the end of month t are $\beta_{\text{SPY,t}} =$ 0.90 and $\text{h}_{\text{t}} = -$0.40. The fund’s trailing 12-month volatility is 14.2%.

| Returns over month t to t + 1 | Return (%) |
|---|---|
| Fund | 1.80 |
| SPY | 1.20 |
| SPYV | 0.50 |
| SPYG | 2.00 |
| US T-bill | 0.20 |

What is the part of the fund’s month t + 1 return not explained by the time-t factor benchmark, that is, $\alpha_{\text{t}} + \epsilon_{\text{t}}+_{1}$?
solution:
A fund-of-funds analyst computes the return not explained by the shorting style benchmark (Equation 3.15).

**Concept and theory**

In Equation (3.15) the benchmark, formed with loadings estimated at t, explains the fund’s excess return over t to t + 1 as

$\beta_{\text{SPY,t}} \left(\text{SPY}_{\text{t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f ,t}+1}\right) + \text{h}_{\text{t}} (\text{SPYV}_{\text{t}}+_{1} - \text{SPYG}_{\text{t}}+_{1})$ .

Rearranging the equation, the part not explained by this benchmark is

$\alpha_{\text{t}} + \epsilon_{\text{t}}+_{1} = \left(\text{r}_{\text{t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f ,t}+1}\right) - \beta_{\text{SPY,t}} \left(\text{SPY}_{\text{t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f ,t}+1}\right) - \text{h}_{\text{t}} (\text{SPYV}_{\text{t}}+_{1} - \text{SPYG}_{\text{t}}+_{1})$ .

question: A risk consultant is advising the investment committee of a Dutch pension fund (EUR 30 billion). Under long-only style analysis, manager X has positive cumulated excess returns trending upward and manager Y has negative cumulated excess returns trending downward. The committee will now re-run both analyses allowing short positions in the ETFs (market excess return plus a SPYV minus SPYG factor). Which outcome is most consistent with the evidence on allowing shorting?

options.A: The overall pattern of cumulated excess returns changes little, but alphas fall: X’s positive excess returns shift down and Y’s trend becomes more negative.
options.B: The overall pattern of cumulated excess returns changes little, but alphas rise: X’s positive excess returns shift up and Y’s trend becomes less negative.
options.C: The overall pattern of cumulated excess returns changes little, but alphas move toward zero: X’s excess returns shift down and Y’s trend becomes less negative.
options.D: The overall pattern of cumulated excess returns changes little, and alphas are unchanged, because allowing shorting alters the style weights but not the benchmark return.

solution:
A consultant predicts how allowing shorting changes two managers’ style-analysis results.

**Concept and theory**

The long-only version (Equation 3.14, Figure 3.5) constrains the weights to sum to one and to be all positive. The shorting version (Equation 3.15, Figure 3.6) lets the benchmark hold short positions, through the excess market return and the long-short SPYV minus SPYG factor. Freeing the benchmark to go short gives it more room to match the fund, so more of the fund’s return tends to be attributed to the benchmark and less is left as alpha. question: A member of the board risk committee of a Japanese non-life insurer (JPY 1.6 trillion of investments) asks the CRO whether style analysis, run on ten years of monthly data, lets the committee conclude with confidence that an external manager adds value. Which response by the CRO is most accurate?

options.A: Style benchmarks fit the fund better each period, so the standard errors of alpha shrink relative to a constant-weight benchmark and significance becomes easier to detect.
options.B: The inference problem is confined to constant-weight benchmarks; once weights vary over time, the usual cutoff of an absolute t-statistic of two is reliable.
options.C: Inference is a serious problem: significance is hard to detect with constant benchmarks even over ten years, and estimated time-varying styles have even larger standard errors.
options.D: Statistical significance is reliably achieved once a sample exceeds ten years, so the larger standard errors of time-varying styles are of little practical concern.

solution:
A board member asks whether ten years of style analysis lets the committee conclude a manager adds value.

**Concept and theory**

Alpha is an average excess return, estimated with error; with returns this noisy, a t-statistic above two in absolute value (the 95% threshold) is rare. GARP notes that most factor regressions do not produce significant alphas and that “detecting statistical significance of outperformance is hard, even in samples of more than ten years”: Berkshire’s alpha is significant starting in 1990 but not when the sample starts in 2001. Time-varying benchmarks make this worse. Each period’s weights are themselves estimates, so estimation error in the benchmark adds to the noise in returns (this mechanism is an interpretation; GARP states the result). Risk consultant auditing four statements on contemporaneous and lagged risk-return relations.

Lagged sorts rank stocks on a risk measure estimated over a past window and then measure returns over a future window: they are predictive and tradeable. question: A member of the risk committee at a Japanese life insurer reviews a backtest of the insurer’s JPY equity sleeve. Stocks were grouped at the end of each quarter by betas realized during that quarter, and the highest-beta group earned the highest average return over that same quarter. The member argues that this contradicts the beta anomaly cited in a proposal to tilt the sleeve toward low-beta stocks. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: The member is right: the beta anomaly states that high-beta stocks earn low raw returns in every period, so any positive same-period relation refutes it.
options.B: The member is not right: the CAPM predicts a positive same-period relation, which the data confirm; the anomaly concerns past betas, which predict future betas poorly.
options.C: The member is not right: the same-period relation between beta and returns is also negative in the data, so the backtest is most likely mis-specified.
options.D: The member is right: the result shows that past betas forecast future betas accurately, so a sort on past betas should also deliver higher future returns.

solution:
Risk committee member claiming that a positive same-quarter beta-return relation refutes the beta anomaly.

**Concept and theory**

The CAPM is a statement about expected returns and the beta that applies over the same period. GARP: the CAPM “states that there should be a contemporaneous relation between beta and expected returns. This is exactly what the CAPM predicts!”

|  | Q1 (low) | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 | Q5 (high) |

| Average post-ranking beta | 0.50 | 0.75 | 0.95 | 1.20 | 1.65 |

options.A: BAB can be formed simply as the return difference between the lowest-beta and highest-beta quintiles, since average returns differ sharply across beta quintiles.
options.B: BAB scales its long and short legs to a 15% target volatility, while VOL scales its long and short legs by their pre-ranking betas to unit beta.
options.C: BAB can use all five beta quintiles, because levering up the lowest-beta quintile, whose pre-ranking beta is close to zero, needs only a modest position.

question:
A senior risk analyst at a Hong Kong insurer reviews the reading’s Fama-French plus momentum regression of the BAB and VOL factors, estimated on monthly returns from October 1963 to December 2011. The correlation between the two factors over the sample is −9%.

|  | $\frac{\text{BAB factor}}{\text{Coeff. t-stat}}$ | $\frac{\text{VOL factor}}{\text{Coeff. t-stat}}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha (% per month) | 0.33 1.89 | 0.42 4.37 |
| MKT loading | −0.17 −4.13 | 0.87 38.80 |
| SMB loading | 0.29 5.20 | −0.63 −20.30 |
| HML loading | 0.48 7.85 | 0.20 5.73 |
| UMD loading | 0.09 2.35 | 0.13 6.00 |

Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.A: BAB’s alpha is significant at the 95% level because its t-statistic exceeds the one-tailed critical value of 1.65, so both factors earn significant alphas.
options.B: VOL’s alpha is strongly significant while BAB’s is only borderline at the 95% level, and both factors carry significant value and momentum tilts.
options.C: Because both factors load positively on HML and UMD, the two anomalies are largely one value and momentum effect, so holding either factor alone is sufficient.
options.D: BAB’s alpha is strongly significant while VOL’s is only borderline at the 95% level, and both factors carry significant value and momentum tilts.

solution:
Senior risk analyst interpreting the Fama-French plus momentum regression of the BAB and VOL factors.

**Concept and theory**

Regressing a factor’s returns on the Fama-French factors plus momentum asks whether the factor earns a return (alpha) not explained by market, size (SMB), value (HML) and momentum (UMD) exposures. A t-statistic tests whether a coefficient differs from zero; at the standard 95% level (two-sided) the critical value is about 1.96, so \|t\| = 1.89 corresponds to a p-value of about 0.06. GARP’s reading of the table:

|  | BAB | VOL |

A data-mined result has a signature: it is fragile to small changes in method and it fails to appear in data that were not used to find it. The natural test is therefore out-of-sample evidence: different periods, different countries and, most powerfully, different asset classes with their own investors and institutions.

loText: Explain how different macroeconomic risk factors, including economic growth, inflation, and volatility, affect asset returns and risk premiums.
question: A group of newly hired analysts at a large pension fund are discussing how changes in different macroeconomic risk factors are likely to impact the fixed-income and equity positions in the fund’s portfolios. The analysts consider the effects of some of the most commonly modeled macroeconomic risk factors, including economic growth, inflation, and volatility, on different classes of stocks and bonds. Which of the following observations is correct for the analysts to make?

options.A: Government bonds tend to generate lower returns during recessionary periods than during expansionary periods.
options.B: Corporate bonds tend to be less volatile during periods of high real gross domestic product (GDP) growth than during periods of low real GDP growth.
options.C: Large-capitalization stocks tend to generate higher returns during periods of high inflation than during periods of low inflation.
options.D: Small-capitalization stocks tend to be more volatile during periods of high consumption growth than during periods of low consumption growth.

solution:
**Concept**

Macro factors. Growth: in high growth equities and corporate bonds do well and are less volatile; in recessions government bonds do well. Inflation: high inflation is bad for both stocks and bonds. Volatility: rising volatility hurts risky assets.

**Exam trap.** Each wrong option reverses one relationship. High inflation lowers stock returns, and high consumption growth lowers stock volatility.

|---|---|---|---|

Which of the following is the best investment avenue for investors in country Y?

options.A: High-yield bonds
options.B: Government bonds
options.C: Investment-grade corporate and local municipal bonds
options.D: Stocks

solution:
**Concept**

Macroeconomic factors and asset returns. Economic growth: equities and high-yield bonds do well in high growth; government bonds do well in low growth. Inflation: high inflation hurts both stocks and bonds. Volatility: when volatility rises, equities fall and investors move to safe government bonds.

question:
A risk analyst is evaluating an investment portfolio using the Fama-French three- factor model. The analyst regresses thirty years of weekly portfolio returns against the three factors of the model. The analyst obtains the following regression results:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Alpha | 0.10 |
| Market coefficient | 0.52 |
| SMB coefficient | 0.18 |
| HML coefficient | -0.70 |

Assuming all estimated coefficients are statistically significant, which of the following is correct?

options.A: There is a positive correlation between portfolio return and the size factor, which indicates that the portfolio moves together with large-cap stocks.
options.B: There is a positive correlation between portfolio return and the value factor, which indicates that the portfolio moves together with growth stocks.
options.C: There is a negative correlation between portfolio return and the size factor, which indicates that the portfolio moves together with large-cap stocks.
options.D: There is a negative correlation between portfolio return and the value factor, which indicates that the portfolio moves together with growth stocks.

solution:
**Concept**

Fama-French three-factor model: $R - R_{f} = \alpha+ \beta_{MKT}(R_{M} - R_{f}) + s$ SMB $+ h$ HML. SMB is small minus big: a positive loading means the portfolio behaves like small-cap stocks. HML is high minus low book-to-market: a positive loading means value, a negative loading means growth.

**Exam trap.** Each option has two parts: the sign and the interpretation. Read the factor names literally: Small Minus Big, High Minus Low. A positive loading sides with the first word.

**Concept**

The low-risk anomaly: stocks with low volatility or low beta have earned higher risk-adjusted returns than high-risk stocks. Low-risk strategies show significant alpha against market-capitalisation benchmarks and also against factor benchmarks that include value and momentum.

**Exam trap.** Alpha always depends on the benchmark, but for the low-risk anomaly the alpha survives the usual factor adjustments.

**Exam trap.** Absolute-claim trap in options A and C (“all”, “must”). Sign check first: positive beta gains in a rising market, negative beta loses.
